How warm will
Hanoi be tomorrow?

Forecasting Hanoi's daily mean temperature 1–7 days ahead from 21 years of weather history — with a close eye on the winter cold surges that make forecasting hard.

Notebook on GitHub ↗ PDF report ↗ Video on YouTubecoming soon
7,939days of Hanoi weather, 2005–2026
0.92 °Ctest MAE, 1 day ahead
15.3%lower error than “tomorrow = today” (1.08 °C)
4 dayshorizon where the model beats every baseline

The problem

Predict tomorrow's daily mean temperature in Hanoi from today's and past weather, then measure how fast forecast skill decays up to a week ahead.

Hanoi has a real winter: north-east monsoon cold surges can cut the temperature by 5–10 °C within a day — exactly the days when a forecast matters most. Models are compared against persistence, climatology and damped-anomaly baselines on a strictly chronological split.

1. Dataset: how it was collected¶

The data was downloaded by the group from the Open-Meteo Historical Weather API (free, no API key; data licensed CC BY 4.0, "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com"). Open-Meteo serves the ERA5 / ERA5-Land reanalysis of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts: a physically consistent reconstruction of past weather on a ~9–25 km grid, built by combining a weather model with millions of historical observations.

  • Location: central Hanoi (21.03 °N, 105.85 °E; the API snaps to the nearest grid cell at 21.05 °N, 105.90 °E, elevation 19 m)
  • Period: 1 Jan 2005 – 26 Sep 2026, daily, local time (GMT+7)
  • 14 variables (below). The function in the next cell is the exact request used; it only runs when REFRESH_FROM_API = True, so Run all uses the saved CSV and gives reproducible results.
Variable Unit Meaning
temperature_2m_mean / _max / _min °C daily mean / max / min air temperature at 2 m — target: mean
apparent_temperature_mean °C "feels-like" temperature
precipitation_sum, precipitation_hours mm, h daily rain total and rainy hours
relative_humidity_2m_mean, dew_point_2m_mean %, °C moisture
pressure_msl_mean hPa mean sea-level pressure
cloud_cover_mean % cloud cover
wind_speed_10m_max, wind_direction_10m_dominant km/h, ° max wind speed and dominant direction
shortwave_radiation_sum, sunshine_duration MJ/m², s solar energy and sunshine

REFRESH_FROM_API = False
DAILY_VARS = ["temperature_2m_mean", "temperature_2m_max", "temperature_2m_min", "apparent_temperature_mean",
              "precipitation_sum", "precipitation_hours", "relative_humidity_2m_mean", "dew_point_2m_mean",
              "pressure_msl_mean", "cloud_cover_mean", "wind_speed_10m_max", "wind_direction_10m_dominant",
              "shortwave_radiation_sum", "sunshine_duration"]


def fetch_open_meteo(lat=21.0285, lon=105.8542, start="2005-01-01", end="2026-09-26"):
    """Download daily history for one location from the Open-Meteo archive API."""
    import requests
    params = dict(latitude=lat, longitude=lon, start_date=start, end_date=end,
                  daily=",".join(DAILY_VARS), timezone="Asia/Bangkok")
    resp = requests.get("https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive", params=params, timeout=180)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return pd.DataFrame(resp.json()["daily"]).rename(columns={"time": "date"})


if REFRESH_FROM_API:
    fetch_open_meteo().to_csv(LOCAL_DATA, index=False)

Finding (figure 2.1). Summer (Jun–Aug) averages 28.7 °C and winter (Dec–Feb) 17.4 °C — an 11 °C seasonal swing. Winter is also far more variable: the standard deviation within January is 3.40 °C vs 1.62 °C in July, and the mean day-to-day change peaks in February–March (1.42–1.49 °C) vs 0.78 °C in July. Forecasting will therefore be hardest in winter and spring, when cold surges and warm spells alternate.

Finding (figure 2.2). Annual mean temperature rises by +0.49 °C per decade over 2005–2025; 2021–25 averaged 24.13 °C vs 23.50 °C in 2005–09 (+0.63 °C). The heatmap shows the large cold anomalies concentrated in the early years (Feb 2008 and Jan–Feb 2011, two long cold spells in northern Vietnam), while recent years are mostly warm. Caveat: 21 years is short and year-to-year swings are large (22.3 °C in 2011 vs 24.6 °C in 2019), so the exact slope is uncertain. Consequence for modelling: a climatology learned on 2005–2021 will be slightly too cold for 2024–2026 (checked in section 5.1).

2.3 How much does today tell us about tomorrow? (autocorrelation)¶

In [7]:
def acf(x, max_lag):
    x = np.asarray(x) - np.mean(x)
    denom = np.dot(x, x)
    return np.array([np.dot(x[:-k], x[k:]) / denom if k else 1.0 for k in range(max_lag + 1)])

clim_doy = t.groupby(doy).transform("mean")
anomaly = t - clim_doy
lags_long = acf(t.values, 800)
lags_anom = acf(anomaly.values, 30)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 3.8))
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(range(801), lags_long, color=PALETTE[0])
ax.axhline(0, color=AXIS, linewidth=1)
for k in (365, 730):
    ax.annotate(f"lag {k}: {lags_long[k]:.2f}", (k, lags_long[k]), xytext=(0, 10), textcoords="offset points", ha="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlabel("Lag (days)"); ax.set_ylabel("Autocorrelation"); ax.set_title("ACF of temperature — the yearly cycle")
ax = axes[1]
ax.bar(range(31), lags_anom, color=PALETTE[1], width=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=AXIS, linewidth=1)
for k in (1, 7):
    ax.text(k, lags_anom[k] + 0.03, f"{lags_anom[k]:.2f}", ha="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlabel("Lag (days)"); ax.set_title("ACF of the anomaly (seasonal cycle removed)")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
savefig("ts_04_acf")
plt.show()

Finding (figure 2.3). The raw series is dominated by the yearly cycle (autocorrelation 0.71 at lag 365). Once the season is removed, the anomaly still has strong day-to-day memory (0.81 at lag 1), but it fades to 0.11 by lag 7: a warm or cold spell "remembers" itself for only a few days. Beyond about a week, the only predictable part is the season itself — a prediction tested directly in section 6.

2.4 Can we see a cold surge coming?¶

Question: in the cold season (Nov–Mar), does a rise in sea-level pressure today warn of a temperature drop tomorrow? A cold surge is a mass of cold, dense (high-pressure) air pushing south from Siberia and China.

In [8]:

ax.axvline(3, color=MUTED, linewidth=1)

      f"vs {w.loc[~big_rise, 'dT_next'].mean():+.2f} °C otherwise; P(drop > 2 °C) = {(w.loc[big_rise, 'dT_next'] < -2).mean():.0%} "

Days with pressure rise > 3 hPa: 404 | mean ΔT tomorrow: -1.03 °C vs +0.15 °C otherwise; P(drop > 2 °C) = 26% vs 10%

Finding (figure 2.4). Yes — the correlation is r = −0.36. On the 404 cold-season days when pressure rose by more than 3 hPa, the next day cooled by 1.03 °C on average (vs +0.15 °C otherwise), and a drop of more than 2 °C was 2.7× as likely (26.5% vs 9.6%). Pressure change over 1 and 3 days therefore becomes a feature.

3. Data preparation¶

3.1 Continuity and missing values¶

A time series must be checked for missing dates, not only missing cells — a skipped day would silently shift every lag feature.

In [9]:

    "days in full calendar range": len(full_range),
    "missing dates": len(full_range.difference(df.index)),

The reanalysis is complete — no missing dates or cells. Real station data is rarely this clean (sensor outages, transmission gaps), so we use the complete series as ground truth for an experiment.

Question: if a weather station lost data for a few days, which imputation method would reconstruct the temperature best — and does the answer depend on gap length?

We hide random blocks of 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 consecutive days (≈5% of the series each time, 5 random repetitions) and compare four methods by MAE on the hidden days:

  1. Forward fill — repeat the last known value.
  2. Linear interpolation — straight line between the values around the gap.
  3. Climatology — the average temperature for that day of the year.
  4. Seasonal interpolation — interpolate the anomaly (value minus climatology) linearly, then add the climatology back.
In [10]:
def make_gaps(n, gap_len, frac=0.05, seed=0):
    """Boolean mask with random non-overlapping blocks of `gap_len` days covering ~frac of n."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mask = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool)
    n_blocks = max(1, int(frac * n / gap_len))
    starts = rng.choice(np.arange(30, n - gap_len - 30), size=n_blocks * 3, replace=False)
    placed = 0
    for s in starts:
        if not mask[max(0, s - 1): s + gap_len + 1].any():
            mask[s: s + gap_len] = True
            placed += 1
            if placed == n_blocks:
                break
    return mask


def impute(series, mask, method, clim):
    s = series.copy()
    s[mask] = np.nan
    if method == "Forward fill":
        return s.ffill()
    if method == "Linear interpolation":
        return s.interpolate(method="time")
    if method == "Climatology":
        return s.fillna(clim)
    if method == "Seasonal interpolation":
        return (s - clim).interpolate(method="time") + clim
    raise ValueError(method)


METHODS = ["Forward fill", "Linear interpolation", "Climatology", "Seasonal interpolation"]
GAP_LENGTHS = [1, 3, 7, 14, 30]
clim_series = pd.Series(clim_doy.values, index=t.index)
rows = []
for gap in GAP_LENGTHS:
    for seed in range(5):
        mask = make_gaps(len(t), gap, seed=seed)
        for m in METHODS:
            filled = impute(t, mask, m, clim_series)
            rows.append({"gap": gap, "method": m, "mae": np.mean(np.abs(filled[mask] - t[mask]))})
imp_res = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby(["gap", "method"])["mae"].mean().unstack()[METHODS]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4))
for i, m in enumerate(METHODS):
    ax.plot(imp_res.index, imp_res[m], marker="o", markersize=6, color=PALETTE[i], label=m)
    ax.annotate(f"{imp_res[m].iloc[-1]:.2f}", (imp_res.index[-1], imp_res[m].iloc[-1]), xytext=(8, 0),

Finding (figure 3.1). For short gaps, seasonal interpolation is best (MAE 0.70 / 1.13 / 1.63 °C for 1 / 3 / 7-day gaps), marginally ahead of plain linear interpolation (0.71 / 1.14 / 1.69). Forward fill is the worst method at every length. For gaps of 14 days or more, plain climatology wins (1.87 °C) — the anomaly's memory (about a week, figure 2.3) has run out, so the best guess is the seasonal normal. A practical rule: interpolate the anomaly for gaps up to ~1 week, fall back to climatology for longer outages. Our series needs no imputation, but the rule would apply to real station data.

3.2 Outliers¶

Temperature outliers are judged against the season: 12 °C is normal in January but extreme in July. We compute a z-score of each day's anomaly against the day-of-year standard deviation and flag |z| > 3.

In [11]:

Decision. Only 9 days (0.11%) exceed |z| > 3, all of them cold: 16–17 March 2011, 3–7 October 2011 (an early-season cold spell), and 6 and 26 September 2013. They are real weather, not sensor errors, and they are exactly the events a forecast must handle → kept. The record 6.1 °C of January 2016 is not even flagged, because January is naturally so variable (std 3.4 °C). Precipitation has 1,001 IQR outliers and skew 5.2; heavy-rain days are also real, so we keep them and feed log1p(rain) to the models (skew 0.95).

3.3 Feature engineering, encoding and scaling (WeatherFeatureBuilder class)¶

For a forecast issued at the end of day t for day t + h, every feature must be known at day t. The class below builds:

Group Features Notes
Recent temperature t_0 (today), lags 1, 2, 3, 7, 14; rolling means over 3, 7, 30 days; today's max, min and diurnal range rolling windows end at day t — no future values
Anomaly anom_0 = today − climatology climatology is learned from the training years only
Weather today humidity, dew point, pressure, pressure change over 1 and 3 days, cloud cover, wind speed, rain (log1p), radiation, sunshine hours
Calendar of the target day doy_sin, doy_cos (cyclical encoding), climatology of the target day
Categorical season of the target day (DJF/MAM/JJA/SON), wind_sector (N, NE, …, NW) one-hot encoded in the pipeline
Wind direction (numeric) wind_sin, wind_cos direction is circular: 359° is next to 1°

Numerical features are standardised with StandardScaler inside the pipeline (needed by Ridge regression; harmless for trees).

In [12]:
SECTORS = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"]
SEASONS = {12: "DJF", 1: "DJF", 2: "DJF", 3: "MAM", 4: "MAM", 5: "MAM",
           6: "JJA", 7: "JJA", 8: "JJA", 9: "SON", 10: "SON", 11: "SON"}


class WeatherFeatureBuilder:
    """Build a supervised dataset for forecasting TARGET `horizon` days ahead.

    Climatology (smoothed day-of-year mean) is fitted on the training period only,
    so the validation/test years never influence the features.
    """

    def __init__(self, target=TARGET, lags=(1, 2, 3, 7, 14), windows=(3, 7, 30)):
        self.target = target
        self.lags = lags
        self.windows = windows

    def fit(self, frame):
        d = frame.index.dayofyear.where(frame.index.dayofyear <= 365, 365)
        by_doy = frame[self.target].groupby(d).mean().reindex(range(1, 366)).interpolate()
        wrapped = pd.concat([by_doy.iloc[-15:], by_doy, by_doy.iloc[:15]])
        self.clim_ = wrapped.rolling(31, center=True).mean().iloc[15:-15]
        return self

    def climatology(self, index):
        d = index.dayofyear.where(index.dayofyear <= 365, 365)
        return pd.Series(self.clim_.reindex(d).values, index=index)

    def transform(self, frame, horizon=1):
        y_now = frame[self.target]
        X = pd.DataFrame(index=frame.index)
        X["t_0"] = y_now
        for lag in self.lags:
            X[f"t_lag{lag}"] = y_now.shift(lag)
        for w in self.windows:
            X[f"t_mean{w}"] = y_now.rolling(w).mean()
        X["tmax_0"] = frame["temperature_2m_max"]
        X["tmin_0"] = frame["temperature_2m_min"]
        X["dtr_0"] = frame["temperature_2m_max"] - frame["temperature_2m_min"]
        X["anom_0"] = y_now - self.climatology(frame.index)
        X["humidity_0"] = frame["relative_humidity_2m_mean"]
        X["dewpoint_0"] = frame["dew_point_2m_mean"]
        X["pressure_0"] = frame["pressure_msl_mean"]
        X["dp_1d"] = frame["pressure_msl_mean"].diff(1)
        X["dp_3d"] = frame["pressure_msl_mean"].diff(3)
        X["cloud_0"] = frame["cloud_cover_mean"]
        X["wind_speed_0"] = frame["wind_speed_10m_max"]
        rad = np.deg2rad(frame["wind_direction_10m_dominant"])
        X["wind_sin"], X["wind_cos"] = np.sin(rad), np.cos(rad)
        X["wind_sector"] = [SECTORS[int(((d + 22.5) % 360) // 45)] for d in frame["wind_direction_10m_dominant"]]
        X["rain_log_0"] = np.log1p(frame["precipitation_sum"])
        X["radiation_0"] = frame["shortwave_radiation_sum"]
        X["sunshine_0"] = frame["sunshine_hours"]
        target_day = frame.index + pd.Timedelta(days=horizon)
        X["doy_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * target_day.dayofyear / 365.25)
        X["doy_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * target_day.dayofyear / 365.25)
        X["clim_target"] = self.climatology(target_day).values
        X["season"] = [SEASONS[m] for m in target_day.month]
        y = y_now.shift(-horizon).rename("target")
        data = X.join(y).dropna()               # drops warm-up rows (lags/rolling) and the last `horizon` rows
        data["target_date"] = data.index + pd.Timedelta(days=horizon)
        return data


CATEGORICAL = ["season", "wind_sector"]

3.4 Time-based train / validation / test split¶

A random split would let the model train on days after the ones it is tested on — information that never exists at forecast time. We split by the date being forecast:

Set Target dates Used for
Train 2005 – 2021 (17 years) fitting; TimeSeriesSplit cross-validation for tuning
Validation 2022 – 2023 choosing between models
Test 1 Jan 2024 – 26 Sep 2026 final, one-time evaluation
In [13]:
def split(data):
    td = data["target_date"]
    return (data[td <= TRAIN_END], data[(td > TRAIN_END) & (td <= VAL_END)], data[td > VAL_END])


train1, val1, test1 = split(data1)
print({name: f"{len(d):,} days ({d['target_date'].min():%Y-%m-%d} → {d['target_date'].max():%Y-%m-%d})"
       for name, d in [("train", train1), ("validation", val1), ("test", test1)]})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 3))
for (name, d), c in zip([("train", train1), ("validation", val1), ("test", test1)], PALETTE[:3]):
    ax.plot(d["target_date"], d["target"], color=c, linewidth=0.6, label=f"{name} ({len(d):,} days)")
ax.set_ylabel("°C"); ax.set_title("Chronological split — the model never sees the future")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", ncols=3)

4. Modelling¶

4.1 Baselines — the bar every model must clear¶

  • Persistence: tomorrow = today. Hard to beat for 1-day forecasts because temperature changes slowly.
  • Climatology: tomorrow = the average for that calendar day (learned on training years).
  • Damped anomaly persistence: tomorrow = climatology + φ × today's anomaly, with φ = lag-1 autocorrelation of anomalies in the training years. A statistical forecaster's classic baseline.

4.2 The ForecastEvaluator class and machine-learning models¶

  • Ridge regression (linear, scaled features)
  • Random Forest
  • HistGradientBoosting (HGB) predicting the temperature directly
  • HGB predicting the change ΔT = T(t+1) − T(t), then adding today's value back. Trees cannot extrapolate beyond the target range seen in training; a warming climate makes that a real risk, and predicting the change sidesteps it.
In [14]:
class ForecastEvaluator:
    """Collect MAE / RMSE / R² / skill-vs-persistence for many forecasts of the same target."""

    def __init__(self, y_true, persistence):
        self.y_true = np.asarray(y_true)
        self.mae_persistence = mean_absolute_error(self.y_true, persistence)
        self.rows = {}
        self.preds = {}

    def add(self, name, y_pred):
        y_pred = np.asarray(y_pred)
        mae = mean_absolute_error(self.y_true, y_pred)
        self.preds[name] = y_pred
        self.rows[name] = {"MAE": mae, "RMSE": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(self.y_true, y_pred)),
                           "R2": r2_score(self.y_true, y_pred), "skill_vs_persistence": 1 - mae / self.mae_persistence}
        return self

    def table(self):
        return pd.DataFrame(self.rows).T.sort_values("MAE")


def make_pipeline(model, scale=True):
    num = StandardScaler() if scale else "passthrough"
    pre = ColumnTransformer([("num", num, NUMERIC),
                             ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), CATEGORICAL)])
    return Pipeline([("prep", pre), ("model", model)])


class DeltaRegressor(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """Wrap a regressor so it learns target - t_0 (the change) and returns a level forecast."""

    def __init__(self, pipeline):
        self.pipeline = pipeline

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.pipeline.fit(X, np.asarray(y) - X["t_0"].values)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.pipeline.predict(X) + X["t_0"].values


anoms_train = (train1["t_0"] - builder.climatology(train1.index)).values
PHI = float(np.corrcoef(anoms_train[:-1], anoms_train[1:])[0, 1])


def baselines(data, horizon=1):
    return {
        "Persistence": data["t_0"].values,
        "Climatology": data["clim_target"].values,
        "Damped anomaly persistence": (data["clim_target"] + PHI ** horizon * data["anom_0"]).values,
    }


ML_MODELS = {
    "Ridge regression": lambda: make_pipeline(Ridge(alpha=1.0)),
    "Random Forest": lambda: make_pipeline(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED), scale=False),
    "HGB (level)": lambda: make_pipeline(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=SEED), scale=False),
    "HGB (change ΔT)": lambda: DeltaRegressor(make_pipeline(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=SEED), scale=False)),
}

ev_val = ForecastEvaluator(val1["target"], val1["t_0"])
for name, pred in baselines(val1).items():
    ev_val.add(name, pred)
fitted = {}
for name, make in ML_MODELS.items():
    fitted[name] = make().fit(train1[FEATURES], train1["target"])
    ev_val.add(name, fitted[name].predict(val1[FEATURES]))
print(f"φ (lag-1 anomaly autocorrelation, train) = {PHI:.3f}")
val_table = ev_val.table()
val_table.round(4)

4.3 Tuning with time-series cross-validation¶

Ordinary k-fold CV would shuffle days, training on the future. TimeSeriesSplit always trains on earlier folds and validates on the next one (5 expanding windows inside 2005–2021). We tune the best model family (HGB on the change target) with a random search over 20 configurations — the grid includes scikit-learn's defaults — scored by MAE.

In [15]:
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    make_pipeline(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=SEED), scale=False),
    param_distributions={
        "model__learning_rate": [0.03, 0.05, 0.1],
        "model__max_iter": [100, 200, 400, 700],
        "model__max_leaf_nodes": [15, 31, 63],
        "model__min_samples_leaf": [20, 40, 80],
        "model__l2_regularization": [0.0, 0.5, 2.0],
    },
    n_iter=20, cv=tscv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error", random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1,
)
# tuned on the change target, matching the DeltaRegressor used above
search.fit(train1[FEATURES], train1["target"] - train1["t_0"])
default_cv = -cross_val_score(make_pipeline(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=SEED), scale=False),
                              train1[FEATURES], train1["target"] - train1["t_0"], cv=tscv,
                              scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error", n_jobs=-1).mean()
print(f"TimeSeriesSplit CV MAE — default HGB: {default_cv:.4f} | best of search: {-search.best_score_:.4f}")
print("Best params:", {k.replace("model__", ""): v for k, v in search.best_params_.items()})
tuned = DeltaRegressor(search.best_estimator_)   # already refit on all training rows
fitted["HGB ΔT (tuned)"] = tuned
ev_val.add("HGB ΔT (tuned)", tuned.predict(val1[FEATURES]))

fold_rows = []
for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(tscv.split(train1)):
    fold_rows.append({"fold": k + 1, "train until": train1["target_date"].iloc[tr[-1]].date(),
                      "validate": f"{train1['target_date'].iloc[te[0]]:%Y-%m} → {train1['target_date'].iloc[te[-1]]:%Y-%m}"})
display(pd.DataFrame(fold_rows))

Finding (figure 4). Every machine-learning model beats every baseline on 2022–2023:

  • HGB predicting the change is best with MAE 0.906 °C, 18% below persistence (1.105). Predicting the change beats predicting the level with the same algorithm (0.933): the forecast stays anchored on today's value, and trees are never asked to extrapolate outside the temperature range seen in training.
  • Random Forest (0.921) is close; Ridge regression is weakest (0.974) — the useful signals interact non-linearly (e.g. a northerly wind matters mostly in winter).
  • Damped anomaly persistence barely improves on persistence (1.092), and climatology alone is poor (2.01 °C): for tomorrow, today's weather matters far more than the calendar.
  • Tuning did not transfer. Time-series CV preferred a more regularised configuration (CV MAE 0.928 vs 0.944 for the defaults), but it scored worse on 2022–2023 (0.922 vs 0.906). A 0.015 °C gain on 2007–2021 folds is within year-to-year noise, so we keep the model chosen on validation: HGB (change ΔT) with default hyperparameters.

Test results. On the 1,000 unseen days from January 2024 to September 2026 the final model reaches MAE 0.916 °C, RMSE 1.226 °C, R² 0.935 — 15.3% lower MAE than persistence (1.081) — and the ranking of all models matches validation. The zoom shows the typical failure: on sharp cold-surge drops (late January and late February 2024), both persistence and the model react a day late; the model anticipates only part of the drop.

Finding (5.1).

  • The biggest gains over persistence come in winter and spring — February 1.15 vs 1.61 °C, March 0.82 vs 1.24, December 0.88 vs 1.12. The model is slightly worse than persistence in April (1.10 vs 1.08) and November (1.12 vs 1.01), the transition months.
  • 7 of the 8 worst forecasts are cold surges: the temperature fell 4.6–8.5 °C in one day and the forecast was 4–7 °C too warm. Most were preceded by a pressure rise on the forecast day (up to +4.2 hPa), but the model reacted only partially — the surge's size is not predictable from local data alone. The exception, 29 April 2024, is a hot day the model expected to cool after a 2.3 hPa pressure rise.
  • Residuals average −0.27 °C (forecasts slightly too cold) — consistent with the warming trend of section 2.2: 2024–2026 were warmer than the training years that shaped the model.

5.2 What drives the predicted change?¶

The final model forecasts the change ΔT and adds today's temperature back, so shuffling t_0 would trivially wreck every forecast. We therefore measure permutation importance on the change model itself: how much does the MAE of the predicted ΔT grow when one feature is shuffled?

In [20]:
change_model = final_model.pipeline if isinstance(final_model, DeltaRegressor) else final_model
change_target = test1["target"] - test1["t_0"] if isinstance(final_model, DeltaRegressor) else test1["target"]
perm = permutation_importance(change_model, test1[FEATURES], change_target, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error",
                              n_repeats=5, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
imp = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=FEATURES).sort_values(ascending=False).head(12)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.4))
ax.barh(imp.index[::-1], imp.values[::-1], color=PALETTE[0], height=0.6)
for i, v in enumerate(imp.values[::-1]):
    ax.text(v + imp.max() * 0.01, i, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlabel("Increase in test MAE of the predicted change when the feature is shuffled (°C)")
ax.set_title("Top 12 features for the 1-day change (permutation importance, test)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
savefig("ts_12_importance")
plt.show()

Finding (5.2). The strongest driver of tomorrow's change is today's anomaly (0.300 °C): an unusually warm day tends to cool back towards normal and vice versa (mean reversion). Next is wind_cos (0.196), the north–south component of the wind — a northerly wind (cos ≈ 1) advects cold air, the signature of a cold surge. Rain (0.134) and cloud cover (0.088) follow, as they suppress daytime heating. The 1-day pressure change is used (0.062) but ranks lower than figure 2.4 suggests, because much of its information is already carried by the wind direction.

6. Forecast horizon: how far ahead is the model useful?¶

Question: forecast skill must decay with lead time. At what horizon does our model stop beating simple baselines? We rebuild the features and retrain the final model's configuration for h = 1…7 days, and score every approach on the same test period.

In [21]:
horizon_rows = []
for h in range(1, 8):
    data_h = builder.transform(df, horizon=h)
    tr_h, _, te_h = split(data_h)
    model_h = clone(final_model).fit(tr_h[FEATURES], tr_h["target"])
    preds = {**baselines(te_h, horizon=h), FINAL_NAME: model_h.predict(te_h[FEATURES])}
    for name, p in preds.items():
        horizon_rows.append({"horizon": h, "method": name, "MAE": mean_absolute_error(te_h["target"], p)})
hz = pd.DataFrame(horizon_rows).pivot(index="horizon", columns="method", values="MAE")
hz = hz[["Persistence", "Climatology", "Damped anomaly persistence", FINAL_NAME]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.4))
for i, col in enumerate(hz.columns):
    ax.plot(hz.index, hz[col], marker="o", markersize=6, color=PALETTE[[1, 3, 2, 0][i]], label=col)
ax.annotate(f"{hz['Persistence'].iloc[-1]:.2f}", (7, hz["Persistence"].iloc[-1]), xytext=(8, 0),
            textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.annotate(f"others ≈ {hz['Climatology'].iloc[-1]:.2f}", (7, hz["Climatology"].iloc[-1]), xytext=(8, -14),
            textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlim(0.7, 7.9)
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 8))
ax.set_xlabel("Forecast horizon (days ahead)"); ax.set_ylabel("Test MAE (°C)")
ax.set_title("Forecast error vs horizon (test 2024 – Sep 2026)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")

Finding (figure 6). The model beats every baseline for 1 to 4 days ahead (MAE 0.92, 1.49, 1.79, 1.95 °C vs the best baseline's 1.08, 1.60, 1.86, 1.97). From day 5 all methods converge on climatology (~1.99 °C): the anomaly memory has faded, exactly as the autocorrelation in figure 2.3 predicted. Persistence becomes worse than simply using the seasonal average from day 3 (2.16 vs 1.99 °C). With local, same-city features only, useful skill lasts about 4 days.

  1. Machine learning beats the classical baselines, but modestly. The final model cuts tomorrow's error by 15% vs "tomorrow = today". Framing the target as the change helped more than hyperparameter tuning did.
  2. The hard days are cold surges. Winter and spring are where the model gains the most, and also where its worst misses happen (4–7 °C too warm on sudden drops). The physical signals — northerly wind, rising pressure, today's anomaly — are what the model learned to use.
  3. Skill fades after ~4 days, when every method converges on the seasonal average. This matches the ~1-week memory of temperature anomalies.
  4. Data preparation lessons: split by time, never randomly; fit the climatology on training years only; for gaps, interpolate the anomaly for short outages and use climatology beyond a week.
  5. Hanoi is warming by about +0.5 °C per decade in this record, enough to leave a −0.27 °C cold bias in forecasts trained on earlier years.

Limitations.

  • ERA5 reanalysis is a smoothed grid-cell value, not a thermometer in the city; real station data would be noisier (urban heat island, sensor gaps).
  • The forecast uses the complete weather of day t; a real forecast issued in the evening would have slightly less information.
  • Only local variables are used. Cold surges start hundreds of kilometres to the north, so their arrival is only partly visible in Hanoi's own data.

Future work. Add upstream features (pressure and temperature in southern China / the northern border provinces a day earlier) to see cold surges coming; use hourly data for a 24-hour forecast; produce probabilistic forecasts (quantile regression) to warn about big drops; compare against the historical output of a physics-based weather model (Open-Meteo also exposes archived forecasts); retrain regularly to track the warming trend.
